One resonant plant, one fixed drive-power budget, and every excitation you might reach for:
**optimal, flat, and shaped multisines** (Schroeder, random, or cophased phase), a **swept
sine**, and **broadband and shaped noise**. Pick any of them and watch two
numbers — and the whole scoreboard — update live, all in your browser, no install.

## The two axes

Every drive here spends the **same total power**. What changes is *how* it spends it, and that
splits cleanly into two independent stories:

- **Time to identify to 5%** — set by the drive's **power spectrum** $P_{xx}(f)$ alone. This is
  the real Cramér–Rao bound (the same Fisher kernel as the [landing-page game](index.qmd) and the
  [`system_ident` pipeline](examples/interactive.qmd)). Pile power where the plant's modal
  parameters are least certain and the clock plummets; spread it flat and you wait ~40× longer.
  Notice that *every* flat-spectrum drive — flat multisine, white noise, a linear sweep — shares
  the **same** time, whatever its phase. Fisher can't tell them apart.

- **Crest factor at the DAC** — set by the **phases**, but *only when the power is spread over many
  lines*. Take a **broadband** multisine (all 120 lines, equal power) and the phase choice swings the
  crest 8×: **random** phases give a noise-like ~3.4, **cophased** lines pile into an impulse (~15)
  that a real actuator would clip, and a **Schroeder** multisine flattens the waveform back toward the
  $\sqrt2$ single-tone floor (~1.9). Crest is measured on the actual samples the DAC would emit — no
  whitening-filter sleight of hand.

## Why the optimal spectrum wins — and where Schroeder actually helps

The champion (★) is the **Fisher-optimal spectrum**, and its win is the *spectrum*, not the phase.
It collapses almost entirely onto **two tones** (all the budget sits on the two resonances —
effective line count ≈ 2). A two-tone drive already has crest ≈ 2 *whatever the phase*, so here
`Optimal · Schroeder` and `Optimal · random phase` come out **identical** — Schroeder is doing no
work. The concentrated spectrum buys you both speed (~40×) and low crest for free.

Schroeder phase earns its keep the moment you are pushed **broadband** — a flat or prior-robust
multisine that deliberately spreads the budget across all 120 lines for robustness. *There*, random
phase gives crest ~3.4 and Schroeder claws it back to ~1.9. So the honest recipe: **optimal spectrum
for speed and naturally low crest; Schroeder phase for when robustness makes you spread the power
out.** Either way a swept sine matches the crest but wastes power off-resonance, and broadband noise
loses on speed (and pays a further leakage / variance penalty for being aperiodic). That is the case
for [optimal excitation](tutorial/why-optimal-excitation.qmd) — something you can *feel* by clicking,
before a single equation.
